source_text: Τῇ ὑπερβολῇ γὰρ τοῦ κρύους ὑπερκαεὶς, πρὸς ἑτέραν καὶ χρόαν καὶ γεῦσιν μετέπεσεν. Καὶ μέντοι καὶ πάλιν λέγεται, ἐπειδὰν γῆς ἐπιτηδείας καὶ ἀέρων εὐκράτων λάβηται, πρὸς τὸ ἀρχαῖον εἶδος ἐπανιέναι. Ὥστε οὐδὲν παρὰ τὸ πρόσταγμα εὕροις ἂν ἐν τοῖς φυομένοις ἐπιτελούμενον. Ἡ δὲ λεγομένη αἶρα, καὶ ὅσα λοιπὰ νόθα σπέρματα τοῖς τροφίμοις ἐγκαταμέμικται, ἅπερ ζιζάνια προσαγορεύειν σύνηθες τῇ Γραφῇ, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ σίτου μεταβολῆς γίνεται, ἀλλ' ἐξ οἰκείας ἀρχῆς ὑπέστη, ἴδιον ἔχοντα γένος. Ἅπερ τὴν εἰκόνα πληροῖ τῶν παραχαρασσόντων τὰ τοῦ Κυρίου διδάγματα, καὶ μὴ γνησίως μαθητευομένων τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πονηροῦ διδασκαλίας διεφθαρμένων, καταμιγνύντων δὲ ἑαυτοὺς τῷ ὑγιαίνοντι σώματι τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, ἵν' ἐκ τοῦ ἀφανοῦς τὰς παρ' ἑαυτῶν βλάβας τοῖς ἀκεραιοτέροις ἐμβάλωσιν. Ἤδη δὲ ὁ Κύριος καὶ τὴν τελείωσιν τῶν εἰς αὐτὸν πεπιστευκότων τῇ τῶν σπερμάτων αὐξήσει παρεικάζει, λέγων· Ὡς ὅταν ἄνθρωπος βάλῃ τὸν σπόρον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ καθεύδῃ, καὶ ἐγείρηται νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν, καὶ ὁ σπόρος ἐγείρηται, καὶ μηκύνηται, ὡς οὐκ οἶδεν αὐτός. Αὐτομάτη γὰρ ἡ γῆ καρποφορεῖ πρῶτον χόρτον, εἶτα στάχυν, εἶτα πλήρη σῖτον ἐν τῷ στάχυϊ. Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην. Καὶ ἐν ἀκαριαίᾳ χρόνου ῥοπῇ ἀπὸ τῆς βλαστήσεως ἀρξαμένη ἡ γῆ, ἵνα φυλάξῃ τοὺς νόμους τοῦ κτίσαντος, πᾶσαν ἰδέαν αὐξήσεως διεξελθοῦσα, εὐθὺς πρὸς τὸ τέλειον ἤγαγε τὰ βλαστήματα. Καὶ λειμῶνες μὲν ἦσαν βαθεῖς τῇ ἀφθονίᾳ τοῦ χόρτου, τῶν δὲ πεδίων τὰ εὔκαρπα φρίσσοντα τοῖς ληΐοις, εἰκόνα πελάγους κυμαίνοντος ἐν τῇ κινήσει τῶν ἀσταχύων ἀπέσωζε. Πᾶσα δὲ βοτάνη καὶ πᾶν λαχανηρὸν γένος, καὶ εἴ τι ἐν φρυγάνοις, καὶ εἴ τι ἐν ὀσπρίοις, κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀφθονίαν τότε τῆς γῆς ὑπερεῖχεν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀπότευγμάτι ἦν ἐν τοῖς τότε προβληθεῖ σιν, οὔτε γεωργῶν ἀπειρίας, οὔτε ἀέρων δυσκρασίας, οὔτε τινὸς ἄλλης αἰτίας τοῖς γινομένοις λυμαινομένης. Οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ ἡ καταδίκη ἐνεπόδιζε τῇ εὐθηνίᾳ τῆς γῆς. Πρεσβύτερα γὰρ ταῦτα τῆς ἁμαρτίας δι' ἣν κατεκρίθημεν, ἐν ἱδρῶτι τοῦ προσώπου ἡμῶν ἐσθίειν τὸν ἄρτον. 5.6 Ἀλλὰ Καὶ ξύλον κάρπιμον, φησὶ, ποιοῦν καρπὸν, οὗ τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ κατὰ γένος καὶ καθ' ὁμοιότητα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ ῥήματι πᾶσαι μὲν λόχμαι κατεπυκνοῦντο· πάντα δὲ ἀνέτρεχε δένδρα, τά τε πρὸς μήκιστον ὕψος διανίστασθαι πεφυκότα, ἐλάται καὶ κέδροι, καὶ κυπάρισσοι καὶ πεῦκαι· πάντες δὲ θάμνοι εὐθὺς ἦσαν ἀμφίκομοι καὶ δασεῖς· καὶ τὰ στεφανωματικὰ λεγόμενα τῶν φυτῶν, αἵ τε ῥωδωνιαὶ καὶ μυρσίναι καὶ δάφναι, πάντα ἐν μιᾷ καιροῦ ῥοπῇ, οὐκ ὄντα πρότερον ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς, εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρῆλθε, μετὰ τῆς οἰκείας ἕκαστον ἰδιότητος, ἐναργεστάταις μὲν διαφοραῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἑτερογενῶν χωριζόμενον, οἰκείῳ δὲ ἕκαστον γνωριζόμενον χαρακτῆρι. Πλήν γε ὅτι τὸ ῥόδον τότε ἄνευ ἀκάνθης ἦν, ὕστερον δὲ τῷ κάλλει τοῦ ἄνθους ἡ ἄκανθα παρεζεύχθη, ἵνα τῷ τερπνῷ τῆς ἀπολαύσεως ἐγγύθεν ἔχωμεν παρακειμένην τὴν λύπην, μεμνημένοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας, δι' ἣν ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους ἡμῖν ἀνατέλλειν κατεδικάσθη ἡ γῆ. Ἀλλὰ προσετάχθη, φησὶ, Ξύλον κάρπιμον, ποιοῦν καρπὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, οὗ τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ, ἐκδοῦναι ἡ γῆ· πολλὰ δὲ τῶν δένδρων ὁρῶμεν οὔτε καρποῖς οὔτε σπέρματι κεχρημένα.
thought_title: The earth's first vegetation and the seed-bearing trees
orientation: Basil is explaining the third day of creation, arguing that every plant and tree came forth at God's command with its own seed and kind, not by transformation from one kind into another.
pass_a_gloss: For by the excess of the cold it was burned, and it changed to another color and taste. And indeed it is also said again, whenever it takes hold of suitable earth and temperate airs, to return to the ancient form. So that you would find nothing accomplished in the things that grow contrary to the command. But the so-called darnel, and as many other bastard seeds as are mixed in with the edible ones, which the Scripture is accustomed to call tares, does not come from the change of the wheat, but came into being from its own beginning, having its own kind. Which things fill the image of those who counterfeit the teachings of the Lord, and who are not genuinely discipled to the word, but who are corrupted from the teaching of the evil one, and who mix themselves into the healthy body of the Church, in order that from the unseen they may cast their own harms into the more innocent. And already the Lord also likens the perfecting of those who have believed in him to the growth of seeds, saying: As when a man casts the seed upon the earth, and sleeps, and rises night and day, and the seed rises, and lengthens, as he himself does not know. For the earth bears fruit of itself, first grass, then ear, then full grain in the ear. Let the earth sprout herbage. And in the turn of a moment of time the earth, having begun from the sprouting, in order that it might keep the laws of the Creator, having passed through every form of growth, immediately brought the sprouts to the perfect state. And the meadows were deep with the abundance of grass, and the fruitful parts of the plains, bristling with the standing crops, preserved the image of a waving sea in the movement of the ears of grain. And every herb and every kind of vegetable, and whatever is among the brushwood, and whatever is among the pulses, then exceeded over the earth in every abundance. For neither was there any failure among the things then brought forth, neither of farmers' inexperience, nor of bad temperament of airs, nor of any other cause harming the things that came into being. Nor indeed did the condemnation hinder the fertility of the earth. For these things are older than the sin through which we were condemned to eat the bread in the sweat of our face. But also, it says, a fruit-bearing tree, making fruit, whose seed is in it according to kind and according to likeness upon the earth. At this word all thickets were made dense; and all trees ran up, both those that are by nature able to rise to greatest height, firs and cedars, and cypresses and pines; and all shrubs were immediately leafy on both sides and shaggy; and the so-called garland-making plants, both rose-beds and myrtles and laurels, all in one turn of the moment, not being before above the earth, passed into being, each with its own peculiarity, separated by clearest differences from the things of other kinds, and each recognized by its own character. Except that the rose then was without thorn, but later the thorn was yoked to the beauty of the flower, in order that we might have the grief lying near to the delight of enjoyment, remembering the sin, through which the earth was condemned to sprout thorns and thistles for us. But it was commanded, it says, that the earth bring forth a fruit-bearing tree, making fruit upon the earth, whose seed is in it; but we see many of the trees using neither fruits nor seed.

choices.why: The verb means to burn or scorch; the prefix hyper- indicates excess, matching the preceding mention of excess of cold.
Nothos means illegitimate or spurious; 'bastard' preserves the contrast with genuine edible seeds.
The verb means to falsify or debase, especially coinage; 'counterfeiting' captures the image of false teaching passing as genuine.
Akeraios means unmixed or simple; comparative form indicates those more vulnerable in the Church.
The verb means to bristle or stand on end; it vividly describes fields thick with standing grain.
The compound means having foliage on both sides or all around; it describes dense shrubs.

pass_b_english: For when it is burned by excess of cold, it changes to another color and taste. And indeed it is said that when it finds suitable soil and temperate air, it returns to its original form. So you would find nothing among growing things that comes to pass apart from the command. But the so-called darnel, and all the other bastard seeds mixed in with the nourishing ones—which Scripture customarily calls tares—do not come from a change in the wheat, but arise from their own origin, having their own kind. These fill out the image of those who counterfeit the Lord's teachings and are not genuinely discipled by the word, but are corrupted by the teaching of the evil one and mix themselves into the healthy body of the Church, so that from hiding they may inflict their own harms on the more innocent. Already the Lord also likens the perfecting of those who have believed in him to the growth of seeds, saying: "As when a man casts the seed on the ground, and sleeps, and rises night and day, and the seed rises and lengthens, he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit by itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" (Mark 4:26-28). "Let the earth bring forth vegetation" (Genesis 1:11). And in the briefest moment of time, the earth began from the sprouting, so that it might keep the laws of its Creator, and passing through every form of growth, it immediately brought the sprouts to completion. The meadows were deep with the abundance of grass, and the fruitful plains, bristling with standing crops, preserved the image of a swelling sea in the movement of the ears of grain. Every herb and every kind of vegetable, and whatever belongs to brushwood and whatever belongs to pulses, then abounded on the earth in all abundance. For there was no failure among the things then brought forth: neither the inexperience of farmers, nor the harshness of the air, nor any other cause was harming what came to be. Nor indeed did the condemnation hinder the fertility of the earth. For these things are older than the sin for which we were condemned to eat our bread in the sweat of our face (Genesis 3:19).

But also, he says, "a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit, whose seed is in it according to kind and according to likeness upon the earth" (Genesis 1:11). At this word all the thickets grew dense; all the trees sprang up—those that by nature rise to the greatest height, firs and cedars, cypresses and pines. All the shrubs were at once leafy on both sides and thick. And the plants called garland-making—the rosebeds and myrtles and laurels—all in one moment of time, not previously existing above the earth, came into being, each with its own proper character, separated by the clearest differences from those of other kinds, and each recognized by its own mark. Except that the rose was then without a thorn; later the thorn was yoked to the beauty of the flower, so that close beside the delight of enjoyment we might have the grief placed nearby, remembering the sin for which the earth was condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles for us (Genesis 3:18). But it was commanded, he says, that the earth put forth "a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit upon the earth, whose seed is in it." Yet we see many trees that have neither fruit nor seed.

problems.quote: surpassed the earth in all abundance
problems.source_quote: κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀφθονίαν τότε τῆς γῆς ὑπερεῖχεν
problems.why: ὑπερεῖχεν means 'excelled, abounded,' not 'surpassed the earth.' The herbs abounded *on* the earth in all abundance.
problems.fix: abounded on the earth in all abundance
problems.ruling: τότε τῆς γῆς is temporal ('then the earth'), not a comparison object. 'Surpassed the earth' misreads the syntax.

edits.old: surpassed the earth in all abundance
edits.new: abounded on the earth in all abundance

fixed: Corrected 'surpassed the earth in all abundance' to 'abounded on the earth in all abundance' because the source 'ὑπερεῖχεν' means 'excelled, abounded,' not 'surpassed the earth.'

last_rejected.why: The Greek βοτάνην is "grass/herb" not "vegetation"; Genesis 1:11 LXX has βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου, but here Basil quotes only βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ βοτάνην. "Vegetation" is too broad; "grass" or "herb" is required.
last_rejected.ruling: βοτάνην covers herb/grass/vegetation; 'vegetation' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: not previously existing above the earth
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐκ ὄντα πρότερον ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς
last_rejected.why: ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς means "upon/over the earth" (spatial), not "above the earth" in the sense of altitude; these plants came into existence on the earth's surface, not that they were previously non-existent above ground level. The phrase means "not previously existing on the earth."
last_rejected.fix: not previously existing on the earth
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς can mean 'above/over the earth'; 'above the earth' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: we might have the grief placed nearby
last_rejected.why: ἔχωμεν is hortatory subjunctive "let us have" or "we should have," not "we might have" as a mere possibility; this is an exhortation or purpose clause (ἵνα + subjunctive), so "we might" weakens the force. "Let us have" or "we should have" is better.
last_rejected.fix: we should have grief placed nearby
last_rejected.ruling: ἵνα + subjunctive purpose clause; 'we might have' is standard English for purpose clauses, not weakened.

last_rejected.quote: Yet we see many trees that have neither fruit nor seed
last_rejected.source_quote: πολλὰ δὲ τῶν δένδρων ὁρῶμεν οὔτε καρποῖς οὔτε σπέρματι κεχρημένα
last_rejected.why: The English omits the key problem: these trees are used/characterized by (κεχρημένα) neither fruit nor seed — the point is that they lack both, contradicting the command. "Have" is too weak; "make use of" or "are furnished with" or "possess" is needed, and the rhetorical point about contradiction is weakened.
last_rejected.fix: Yet we see many trees furnished with neither fruit nor seed
last_rejected.ruling: κεχρημένα with dative here means 'having/furnished with'; 'have neither fruit nor seed' captures the meaning adequately.
